PATERNITY ACTION (PETITION TO ESTABLISH PARENTAL RELATIONSHIP) INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Lee

PETITIONER — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF PETITION TO ESTABLISH PARENTAL RELATIONSHIP
I, Jordan Alex Lee, seek to establish, through the California court process described in this document, the parent-child relationship between Morgan Lee and Riley Lee, a minor born May 3, 2015. Riley Lee's other parent or presumed parent of record, so far as known, is Casey Lee. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition to establish (or, where applicable, to determine the nonexistence of) a parental relationship, to be filed in California superior court under the Uniform Parentage Act, Family Code Division 12, Part 3. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not establish, disestablish, or confirm Morgan Lee's legal parentage of Riley Lee. Only a court judgment issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process — which may include court-ordered genetic testing — can actually establish or disestablish that relationship.

THIS PETITION INFORMATION SHEET DESCRIBES A CONTESTED COURT PROCESS, NOT THE VOLUNTARY DECLARATION
California recognizes two distinct routes to legally establishing a parent-child relationship. One is the out-of-court, signed voluntary declaration of parentage described in a separate companion document, which depends on both people agreeing to sign. The other — the subject of this information sheet — is a contested court proceeding under California's Uniform Parentage Act (Fam. Code Div. 12, Part 3), used when parentage is disputed or when a party will not voluntarily sign a declaration. Family Code § 7630(a) authorizes specified people to "bring an action" in court to declare the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship regarding Riley Lee. Completing this information sheet does not itself establish or disestablish Morgan Lee's parentage of Riley Lee; only a court judgment issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process under the Uniform Parentage Act can do that.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A child, the child’s natural mother, a person presumed to be the child’s parent under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, a person seeking to be adjudicated as a parent or donor under Section 7613, an adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished, or a prospective adoptive parent of the child may bring an action as follows:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a) (California Legislative Information text), the introductory clause identifying who may bring an action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7630.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can maintain two legally distinct pathways to establishing parentage — an out-of-court signed declaration and a separate contested court action — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific child's situation, nor a claim that every jurisdiction structures its parentage law this same way. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 7630(a) introductory clause); no additional independent source was found for this specific framing. Whether a voluntary out-of-court declaration process exists at all, whether a separate contested court action exists, and how the two interact varies by state.

WHO MAY BRING AN ACTION TO ESTABLISH OR DISESTABLISH PARENTAGE
California's Uniform Parentage Act lists specific categories of people who may file a court action to determine parentage; not everyone with an interest in Riley Lee's parentage has standing to do so. Family Code § 7630(a) authorizes the child, the child's natural mother, a person already presumed to be the child's parent under specific marital or holding-out categories, a person seeking to be adjudicated a parent or donor in an assisted-reproduction context, an adoption agency, or a prospective adoptive parent to bring an action regarding the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship. Separately, § 7630(c) authorizes a broader general "action to determine parentage" — outside the marital-presumption chapter — to be brought by the child, a personal representative of the child, the Department of Child Support Services, a presumed parent (or that parent's representative if the presumed parent has died or is a minor), and, only when the natural mother is the only presumed parent, a dependency action is pending, or an adoption is pending, a man alleged or claiming to be the father (or his representative if he has died or is a minor).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A child, the child’s natural mother, a person presumed to be the child’s parent under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, a person seeking to be adjudicated as a parent or donor under Section 7613, an adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished, or a prospective adoptive parent of the child may bring an action as follows:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a) (California Legislative Information text), standing to bring an action regarding existence or nonexistence of the relationship (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7630.)
  "Except as to cases coming within Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 7540) of Part 2 or when paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) applies, an action to determine parentage may be brought by the child, a personal representative of the child, the Department of Child Support Services, a presumed parent or the personal representative or a parent of that presumed parent if that parent has died or is a minor, or, when the natural mother is the only presumed parent or an action under Section 300 of the Welfare and Institutions Code or adoption is pending, a man alleged or claiming to be the father or the personal representative or a parent of the alleged father if the alleged father has died or is a minor."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(c) (California Legislative Information text), standing for a general action to determine parentage, including DCSS and a conditioned alleged-father category (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7630.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state can define a specific, limited list of people with standing to bring a contested parentage action — not a claim about which state's law governs standing in any specific case, nor a claim that any particular person does or does not have standing. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7630(a) and § 7630(c)); no additional independent source beyond § 7630 itself was found for this list. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: an alleged father's standing to bring a general parentage action under § 7630(c) is not unconditional — the statute's own text limits it to circumstances where the natural mother is the only presumed parent, or a Welfare and Institutions Code § 300 dependency action or an adoption is pending. Who has standing to bring a contested parentage action, and under what conditions, varies by state.

THE MARITAL PRESUMPTION AND ITS TWO-YEAR DEADLINE TO DISESTABLISH
California law starts from a strong marital presumption: Family Code § 7540(a) provides that, except as provided in § 7541, "the child of spouses who cohabited at the time of conception and birth is conclusively presumed to be a child of the marriage." That presumption is not absolute. Section 7541(a) provides that if the court finds, based on genetic testing, that the spouse presumed to be a parent under § 7540 is not a genetic parent of the child, the question of parentage is resolved under the Uniform Parentage Act's other applicable provisions. But § 7541(b) attaches a firm outer deadline to that challenge: "An action to challenge the parentage of the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 shall be filed and served not later than two years from the child's date of birth," and may be filed only by either spouse, or by a person presumed to be a parent under § 7611, or by the child (through a guardian ad litem) to establish that § 7611-presumed person's parentage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in Section 7541, the child of spouses who cohabited at the time of conception and birth is conclusively presumed to be a child of the marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7540(a) (California Legislative Information text), the conclusive marital presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7540.)
  "If the court finds that the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 is not a genetic parent of the child pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 7550), the question of parentage shall be resolved in accordance with all other applicable provisions of this division, including, but not limited to, Section 7612."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7541(a) (California Legislative Information text), genetic testing overcoming the presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7541.)
  "An action to challenge the parentage of the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 shall be filed and served not later than two years from the child’s date of birth and may only be filed by any of the following: (1) By either spouse. (2) By a person who is a presumed parent under Section 7611 or by the child, through or by the child’s guardian ad litem, to establish the parentage of the person who is a presumed parent under Section 7611."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7541(b) (California Legislative Information text), the two-year filing deadline and who may bring the challenge (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7541.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can pair a strong, birth-during-marriage presumption of parentage with a fixed, short outer deadline for challenging it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage, birth, or challenge, and not a claim about whether the petitioner, respondent, or alleged parent in any specific matter falls within any of these categories. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 7540(a) and § 7541(a)-(b)); the citations from § 7541 are two subsections of that same section, and no additional independent source beyond § 7541 itself was found for the two-year deadline and who may invoke it. Whether a marital presumption of parentage exists, how strong it is, whether and how it can be rebutted, and any deadline for doing so all vary substantially by state — this is exactly the kind of date-sensitive, jurisdiction-specific rule that does not transfer across state lines.

GENETIC TESTING: WHEN THE COURT MUST ORDER IT, AND THE STATUTORY THRESHOLD FOR IDENTIFYING A GENETIC PARENT
Genetic testing plays a defined, but not unlimited, role in a contested parentage action. Family Code § 7551(a) provides that in a civil action or proceeding in which parentage is a relevant fact, "the court may, upon its own initiative or upon suggestion made by or on behalf of any person who is involved, and shall upon motion of any party to the action or proceeding made at a time so as not to delay the proceedings unduly, order the woman who gave birth, the child, and the alleged genetic parent to submit to genetic testing." Once testing occurs, § 7555(a) sets a specific statistical threshold for what counts as identifying someone as a genetic parent: the testing must disclose "at least a 99 percent probability of parentage, using a prior probability of 0.50," and "a combined relationship index of at least 100 to 1."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), in a civil action or proceeding in which parentage is a relevant fact, the court may, upon its own initiative or upon suggestion made by or on behalf of any person who is involved, and shall upon motion of any party to the action or proceeding made at a time so as not to delay the proceedings unduly, order the woman who gave birth, the child, and the alleged genetic parent to submit to genetic testing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7551(a) (California Legislative Information text), when the court may, and on a party's motion shall, order genetic testing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7551.)
  "Subject to a challenge under subdivision (b), a person is identified under this part as a genetic parent of a child if genetic testing complies with this part and the results of the testing disclose both of the following: (1) The person has at least a 99 percent probability of parentage, using a prior probability of 0.50, as calculated by using the combined relationship index obtained in the testing. (2) A combined relationship index of at least 100 to 1."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statistical threshold for identifying a genetic parent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7555.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific court-ordered-testing trigger and a specific statistical threshold for genetic-parent identification — not a claim about which state's law governs whether, or under what threshold, genetic testing would be ordered or would identify anyone as a genetic parent of any specific child. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 7551(a) and § 7555(a)); each citation is a single subsection of its respective section. Section 7551 itself notes that where the child already has a presumed parent under § 7540 (the marital presumption), a motion for genetic testing is instead governed by § 7541, addressed in this document's companion clause — this clause does not restate that separate pathway. Whether courts order genetic testing, on what trigger, and what statistical threshold identifies a genetic parent all vary by state.

HOW GENETIC TESTING MUST BE PERFORMED: LABORATORY ACCREDITATION AND SPECIMEN TYPES
California law does not leave the reliability of court-ordered genetic testing undefined. Family Code § 7552(a) requires that testing "be of a type reasonably relied on by experts in the field of genetic testing and performed in a testing laboratory accredited by" either the AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) or a successor organization, or an accrediting body designated by the Secretary of the United States Department of Health and Human Services. Section 7552(b) separately specifies what may be tested: a specimen "may consist of a sample or a combination of samples of blood, buccal cells, bone, hair, or other body tissue or fluid," and the specimen type need not be the same for each person tested.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Genetic testing shall be of a type reasonably relied on by experts in the field of genetic testing and performed in a testing laboratory accredited by either of the following: (1) The AABB, formerly known as the American Association of Blood Banks, or a successor organization. (2) An accrediting body designated by the Secretary of the United States Department of Health and Human Services."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7552(a) (California Legislative Information text), the expert-reliability and laboratory-accreditation standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7552.)
  "A specimen used in genetic testing may consist of a sample or a combination of samples of blood, buccal cells, bone, hair, or other body tissue or fluid. The specimen used in the testing need not be of the same kind for each person undergoing genetic testing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7552(b) (California Legislative Information text), permissible specimen types (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7552.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can condition the reliability of genetic-parentage testing on a specific accreditation standard and a defined, but non-exclusive, list of acceptable specimen types — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what standard would apply to, any specific test. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7552(a) and § 7552(b)); they are not independent of one another. Section 7552 also addresses, in subdivisions (c) and (d) (not quoted here), how a testing laboratory selects the ethnic or racial database used to calculate a relationship index, a process a party or local child support agency may object to and ask the court to revisit; this clause does not cover that separate procedure. Whether, and by what standard, genetic parentage testing must be accredited or performed varies by state.

CHALLENGING A GENETIC-PARENT IDENTIFICATION
A person identified as a genetic parent under the statistical threshold described in this document's companion clause on genetic testing does not have unlimited grounds to dispute that identification. Family Code § 7555(b) provides that such a person "may challenge the genetic testing results only by other genetic testing satisfying the requirements of this chapter that either excludes the person as a genetic parent of the child or identifies another person as a possible genetic parent of the child" other than the woman who gave birth or the person challenging parentage. If that further testing itself identifies more than one possible genetic parent other than the woman who gave birth, § 7555(c) provides that "the court shall order each person to submit to further genetic testing to identify a genetic parent."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "A person identified pursuant to subdivision (a) as a genetic parent of the child may challenge the genetic testing results only by other genetic testing satisfying the requirements of this chapter that either excludes the person as a genetic parent of the child or identifies another person as a possible genetic parent of the child other than the woman who gave birth to the child or the person challenging parentage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(b) (California Legislative Information text), the exclusive rebuttal mechanism — further qualifying genetic testing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7555.)
  "If more than one person, other than the woman who gave birth to the child, is identified by genetic testing as a possible genetic parent of the child, the court shall order each person to submit to further genetic testing to identify a genetic parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(c) (California Legislative Information text), further testing where the rebuttal identifies multiple possible parents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7555.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can limit how a genetic-parent identification may be rebutted — to further qualifying genetic testing only — and can provide a specific mechanism for resolving a further test that identifies multiple possible parents, not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any specific identification would be challenged or resolved. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7555(b) and § 7555(c)); they are not independent of one another, and both are subject to the same section's subdivision (a) identification standard, which is addressed in this document's companion clause on genetic testing and not restated here. Whether, and how, a genetic-parent identification can be challenged varies by state.

CONSEQUENCE OF DECLINING A COURT-ORDERED GENETIC TEST
California law attaches a specific consequence to refusing a court-ordered genetic test. Family Code § 7554(a) sets out a framework under which, if the woman who gave birth to Riley Lee is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage of Riley Lee under this division, the court shall find the alleged father or alleged genetic parent to be a parent if that person meets any of several listed conditions — among them, § 7554(a)(3): if the person "[d]eclines to submit to genetic testing ordered by the court or a local child support agency," the court may find that person to be a parent of the child "even if the person denies a genetic relationship with the child."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "If the woman who gave birth to the child is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage of the child under this division, the court shall find the person who is the alleged father or genetic parent who is not a donor under Section 7613 to be a parent of the child if the person meets any of the following:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7554(a) (California Legislative Information text), introductory clause and condition of the § 7554(a) framework (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7554.)
  "Declines to submit to genetic testing ordered by the court or a local child support agency, in which case, the court may find that the person is a parent of the child even if the person denies a genetic relationship with the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7554(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), consequence of declining court-ordered genetic testing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7554.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can attach a specific adverse consequence to declining a court-ordered genetic test — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what any specific court would find regarding, any specific person's refusal. This clause cites two parts of the same statutory subsection (§ 7554(a)'s introductory clause and § 7554(a)(3)); they are not independent of one another — the introductory clause's own condition (that the woman who gave birth is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage) applies to the refusal consequence quoted here. Section 7554(a) lists four other bases (identification under § 7555 that is not successfully challenged, an admission accepted by the court, default, and other evidence) on which a court may likewise find a person to be a parent; this clause addresses only the refusal basis and does not restate those other bases. Whether, and under what conditions, a refusal to submit to testing carries this consequence varies by state.

HOW THE COST OF A COURT-APPOINTED TESTING EXPERT IS FIXED AND ALLOCATED
The cost of genetic testing ordered under a court-appointed expert is not left unaddressed. Family Code § 7553(a) provides that the compensation of each court-appointed expert witness "shall be fixed at a reasonable amount" and paid as the court orders; except as provided in § 7553(b), the court may order it paid by the parties in proportions and at times the court sets, may order a party's proportion paid by the county, and may then tax all, part, or none of that amount as costs in the action. Section 7553(b) draws a distinct line for an expert appointed on the court's own motion rather than at a party's request: "If the expert witness is appointed for the court's needs, the compensation shall be paid by the court."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The compensation of each expert witness appointed by the court shall be fixed at a reasonable amount. It shall be paid as the court shall order. Except as provided in subdivision (b), the court may order that it be paid by the parties in the proportions and at the times the court prescribes, or that the proportion of any party be paid by the county, and that, after payment by the parties or the county or both, all or part or none of it be taxed as costs in the action or proceeding."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7553(a) (California Legislative Information text), fixing and allocating a party-requested expert's compensation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7553.)
  "If the expert witness is appointed for the court’s needs, the compensation shall be paid by the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7553(b) (California Legislative Information text), the court pays for an expert appointed for its own needs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7553.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can both give a court discretion to allocate a testing expert's cost among the parties or the county (and to tax it as costs) and separately require the court itself to bear the cost of an expert it appoints for its own needs — not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any specific testing expert's cost would be allocated in any specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7553(a) and § 7553(b)); they are not independent of one another — subdivision (a) is itself expressly qualified by subdivision (b). Whether, and how, the cost of court-ordered genetic testing is allocated varies by state.

COMPETING PRESUMPTIONS AND GENETIC EVIDENCE — THE "WEIGHTIER CONSIDERATIONS" STANDARD
A person can qualify as a presumed parent under Family Code § 7611 through several routes — marriage or an attempted marriage around the time of the child's birth, later marrying and being named on the birth certificate or undertaking support, or receiving the child into the home and openly holding the child out as the person's own. Section 7612(a) makes that presumption rebuttable, and only "by clear and convincing evidence." Where more than one of these presumptions could apply to Riley Lee, or where a § 7611 presumption conflicts with a claim by a person identified as a genetic parent under § 7555, § 7612(b) does not automatically favor genetic evidence: instead, "the presumption that on the facts is founded on the weightier considerations of policy and logic controls," and if one of the competing presumed parents is also a presumed parent under the marital-presumption statute (§ 7540), that particular presumption can only be rebutted through the § 7541 process described in this document's companion clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 7540) and Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 7570) of Part 2, a presumption under Section 7611 is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof and may be rebutted in an appropriate action only by clear and convincing evidence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7612(a) (California Legislative Information text), rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7612.)
  "If two or more presumptions arise under Section 7611 that conflict with each other, or if one or more presumptions under Section 7611 conflict with a claim by a person identified as a genetic parent pursuant to Section 7555, the presumption that on the facts is founded on the weightier considerations of policy and logic controls. If one of the presumed parents is also a presumed parent under Section 7540, the presumption arising under Section 7540 may only be rebutted pursuant to Section 7541."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7612(b) (California Legislative Information text), the weightier-considerations standard for competing presumptions or genetic evidence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7612.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can resolve competing parentage presumptions — including a conflict with genetic-testing evidence — through a case-specific policy-and-logic balancing test rather than a fixed rule automatically favoring either the presumption or the genetic result, not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any such conflict would be resolved for, any specific child. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7612(a) and § 7612(b)); no additional independent source beyond § 7612 itself was found for the weightier-considerations standard. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: on the statute's actual text, a genetic-parent identification under § 7555 does not itself create a separate rebuttable or conclusive presumption that automatically controls over a conflicting § 7611 presumption — it is instead one input the court weighs under the same weightier-considerations balancing test used for conflicts between two § 7611 presumptions. Whether, and how, competing parentage presumptions and genetic evidence are reconciled varies by state.

TIMING RULES FOR ACTIONS TO ESTABLISH OR DISESTABLISH THE EXISTENCE OF A PARENT-CHILD RELATIONSHIP
California's Uniform Parentage Act does not apply one single statute of limitations to every kind of parentage action; the timing rule depends on what is being asked of the court. Family Code § 7630(a)(1) allows an action "[a]t any time for the purpose of declaring the existence of" a presumed or established parent-child relationship regarding Riley Lee — no fixed filing deadline applies to establishing that relationship under this provision. By contrast, § 7630(a)(2) allows an action to declare the nonexistence of a § 7611(a)-(c) presumed relationship "only if the action is brought within a reasonable time after obtaining knowledge of relevant facts" — a flexible, fact-dependent limit rather than a fixed number of days or years. A different, fixed rule applies specifically to challenging the separate marital presumption under § 7540: as described in this document's companion clause, § 7541(b) requires that specific challenge to be filed and served within a hard two-year deadline running from the child's date of birth.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "At any time for the purpose of declaring the existence of the parent and child relationship presumed under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, or established pursuant to Section 7613."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), no fixed deadline to declare the existence of the relationship (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7630.)
  "For the purpose of declaring the nonexistence of the parent and child relationship presumed under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611 only if the action is brought within a reasonable time after obtaining knowledge of relevant facts. After the presumption has been rebutted, parentage of the child by another person may be determined in the same action, if that person has been made a party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the reasonable-time standard to declare nonexistence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7630.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can apply different timing rules — no deadline, a flexible reasonable-time standard, and a fixed deadline — to different categories of parentage action within a single statutory scheme, not a claim about which state's law governs the timing of any specific petitioner's, respondent's, or alleged parent's claim. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7630(a)(1) and § 7630(a)(2)); the cross-reference to § 7541(b)'s two-year deadline is addressed independently, and in full, in this document's companion clause on the marital presumption, and is not re-quoted here. No general, catch-all limitations period for a § 7630(c) action to determine parentage (outside the marital-presumption and nonexistence-challenge categories addressed above) was located in the sections reviewed for this document; this document does not represent that no such rule exists elsewhere in California law, only that this research did not locate one within the sections reviewed. Whether, and how, a state limits the time to bring or challenge a parentage action varies substantially and is exactly the kind of date-sensitive fact that does not transfer across jurisdictions.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — PATERNITY ACTION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual petition to establish a parental relationship, filed in California superior court under the Uniform Parentage Act. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not establish or disestablish parentage of Riley Lee; only a court judgment does that.]

expectedJSON.body: California's Uniform Parentage Act lists specific categories of people who may file a court action to determine parentage; not everyone with an interest in Riley Lee's parentage has standing to do so. Family Code § 7630(a) authorizes the child, the child's natural mother, a person already presumed to be the child's parent under specific marital or holding-out categories, a person seeking to be adjudicated a parent or donor in an assisted-reproduction context, an adoption agency, or a prospective adoptive parent to bring an action regarding the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship. Separately, § 7630(c) authorizes a broader general "action to determine parentage" — outside the marital-presumption chapter — to be brought by the child, a personal representative of the child, the Department of Child Support Services, a presumed parent (or that parent's representative if the presumed parent has died or is a minor), and, only when the natural mother is the only presumed parent, a dependency action is pending, or an adoption is pending, a man alleged or claiming to be the father (or his representative if he has died or is a minor).

Who has standing to bring a contested parentage action, and under what conditions, varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: California law starts from a strong marital presumption: Family Code § 7540(a) provides that, except as provided in § 7541, "the child of spouses who cohabited at the time of conception and birth is conclusively presumed to be a child of the marriage." That presumption is not absolute. Section 7541(a) provides that if the court finds, based on genetic testing, that the spouse presumed to be a parent under § 7540 is not a genetic parent of the child, the question of parentage is resolved under the Uniform Parentage Act's other applicable provisions. But § 7541(b) attaches a firm outer deadline to that challenge: "An action to challenge the parentage of the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 shall be filed and served not later than two years from the child's date of birth," and may be filed only by either spouse, or by a person presumed to be a parent under § 7611, or by the child (through a guardian ad litem) to establish that § 7611-presumed person's parentage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7540(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the conclusive marital presumption
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 7541, the child of spouses who cohabited at the time of conception and birth is conclusively presumed to be a child of the marriage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7541(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: genetic testing overcoming the presumption
citations.quote: If the court finds that the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 is not a genetic parent of the child pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 7550), the question of parentage shall be resolved in accordance with all other applicable provisions of this division, including, but not limited to, Section 7612.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7541(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the two-year filing deadline and who may bring the challenge
citations.quote: An action to challenge the parentage of the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 shall be filed and served not later than two years from the child’s date of birth and may only be filed by any of the following: (1) By either spouse. (2) By a person who is a presumed parent under Section 7611 or by the child, through or by the child’s guardian ad litem, to establish the parentage of the person who is a presumed parent under Section 7611.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can pair a strong, birth-during-marriage presumption of parentage with a fixed, short outer deadline for challenging it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage, birth, or challenge, and not a claim about whether the petitioner, respondent, or alleged parent in any specific matter falls within any of these categories. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 7540(a) and § 7541(a)-(b)); the citations from § 7541 are two subsections of that same section, and no additional independent source beyond § 7541 itself was found for the two-year deadline and who may invoke it. Whether a marital presumption of parentage exists, how strong it is, whether and how it can be rebutted, and any deadline for doing so all vary substantially by state — this is exactly the kind of date-sensitive, jurisdiction-specific rule that does not transfer across state lines.

expectedJSON.body: Genetic testing plays a defined, but not unlimited, role in a contested parentage action. Family Code § 7551(a) provides that in a civil action or proceeding in which parentage is a relevant fact, "the court may, upon its own initiative or upon suggestion made by or on behalf of any person who is involved, and shall upon motion of any party to the action or proceeding made at a time so as not to delay the proceedings unduly, order the woman who gave birth, the child, and the alleged genetic parent to submit to genetic testing." Once testing occurs, § 7555(a) sets a specific statistical threshold for what counts as identifying someone as a genetic parent: the testing must disclose "at least a 99 percent probability of parentage, using a prior probability of 0.50," and "a combined relationship index of at least 100 to 1."

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7551(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: when the court may, and on a party's motion shall, order genetic testing
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), in a civil action or proceeding in which parentage is a relevant fact, the court may, upon its own initiative or upon suggestion made by or on behalf of any person who is involved, and shall upon motion of any party to the action or proceeding made at a time so as not to delay the proceedings unduly, order the woman who gave birth, the child, and the alleged genetic parent to submit to genetic testing.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statistical threshold for identifying a genetic parent
citations.quote: Subject to a challenge under subdivision (b), a person is identified under this part as a genetic parent of a child if genetic testing complies with this part and the results of the testing disclose both of the following: (1) The person has at least a 99 percent probability of parentage, using a prior probability of 0.50, as calculated by using the combined relationship index obtained in the testing. (2) A combined relationship index of at least 100 to 1.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific court-ordered-testing trigger and a specific statistical threshold for genetic-parent identification — not a claim about which state's law governs whether, or under what threshold, genetic testing would be ordered or would identify anyone as a genetic parent of any specific child. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 7551(a) and § 7555(a)); each citation is a single subsection of its respective section. Section 7551 itself notes that where the child already has a presumed parent under § 7540 (the marital presumption), a motion for genetic testing is instead governed by § 7541, addressed in this document's companion clause — this clause does not restate that separate pathway. Whether courts order genetic testing, on what trigger, and what statistical threshold identifies a genetic parent all vary by state.

expectedJSON.body: California law does not leave the reliability of court-ordered genetic testing undefined. Family Code § 7552(a) requires that testing "be of a type reasonably relied on by experts in the field of genetic testing and performed in a testing laboratory accredited by" either the AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) or a successor organization, or an accrediting body designated by the Secretary of the United States Department of Health and Human Services. Section 7552(b) separately specifies what may be tested: a specimen "may consist of a sample or a combination of samples of blood, buccal cells, bone, hair, or other body tissue or fluid," and the specimen type need not be the same for each person tested.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7552(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the expert-reliability and laboratory-accreditation standard
citations.quote: Genetic testing shall be of a type reasonably relied on by experts in the field of genetic testing and performed in a testing laboratory accredited by either of the following: (1) The AABB, formerly known as the American Association of Blood Banks, or a successor organization. (2) An accrediting body designated by the Secretary of the United States Department of Health and Human Services.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7552(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: permissible specimen types
citations.quote: A specimen used in genetic testing may consist of a sample or a combination of samples of blood, buccal cells, bone, hair, or other body tissue or fluid. The specimen used in the testing need not be of the same kind for each person undergoing genetic testing.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can condition the reliability of genetic-parentage testing on a specific accreditation standard and a defined, but non-exclusive, list of acceptable specimen types — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what standard would apply to, any specific test. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7552(a) and § 7552(b)); they are not independent of one another. Section 7552 also addresses, in subdivisions (c) and (d) (not quoted here), how a testing laboratory selects the ethnic or racial database used to calculate a relationship index, a process a party or local child support agency may object to and ask the court to revisit; this clause does not cover that separate procedure. Whether, and by what standard, genetic parentage testing must be accredited or performed varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: A person identified as a genetic parent under the statistical threshold described in this document's companion clause on genetic testing does not have unlimited grounds to dispute that identification. Family Code § 7555(b) provides that such a person "may challenge the genetic testing results only by other genetic testing satisfying the requirements of this chapter that either excludes the person as a genetic parent of the child or identifies another person as a possible genetic parent of the child" other than the woman who gave birth or the person challenging parentage. If that further testing itself identifies more than one possible genetic parent other than the woman who gave birth, § 7555(c) provides that "the court shall order each person to submit to further genetic testing to identify a genetic parent."

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exclusive rebuttal mechanism — further qualifying genetic testing
citations.quote: A person identified pursuant to subdivision (a) as a genetic parent of the child may challenge the genetic testing results only by other genetic testing satisfying the requirements of this chapter that either excludes the person as a genetic parent of the child or identifies another person as a possible genetic parent of the child other than the woman who gave birth to the child or the person challenging parentage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: further testing where the rebuttal identifies multiple possible parents
citations.quote: If more than one person, other than the woman who gave birth to the child, is identified by genetic testing as a possible genetic parent of the child, the court shall order each person to submit to further genetic testing to identify a genetic parent.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can limit how a genetic-parent identification may be rebutted — to further qualifying genetic testing only — and can provide a specific mechanism for resolving a further test that identifies multiple possible parents, not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any specific identification would be challenged or resolved. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7555(b) and § 7555(c)); they are not independent of one another, and both are subject to the same section's subdivision (a) identification standard, which is addressed in this document's companion clause on genetic testing and not restated here. Whether, and how, a genetic-parent identification can be challenged varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: California law attaches a specific consequence to refusing a court-ordered genetic test. Family Code § 7554(a) sets out a framework under which, if the woman who gave birth to Riley Lee is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage of Riley Lee under this division, the court shall find the alleged father or alleged genetic parent to be a parent if that person meets any of several listed conditions — among them, § 7554(a)(3): if the person "[d]eclines to submit to genetic testing ordered by the court or a local child support agency," the court may find that person to be a parent of the child "even if the person denies a genetic relationship with the child."

citations.quote: If the woman who gave birth to the child is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage of the child under this division, the court shall find the person who is the alleged father or genetic parent who is not a donor under Section 7613 to be a parent of the child if the person meets any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7554(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consequence of declining court-ordered genetic testing
citations.quote: Declines to submit to genetic testing ordered by the court or a local child support agency, in which case, the court may find that the person is a parent of the child even if the person denies a genetic relationship with the child.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can attach a specific adverse consequence to declining a court-ordered genetic test — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what any specific court would find regarding, any specific person's refusal. This clause cites two parts of the same statutory subsection (§ 7554(a)'s introductory clause and § 7554(a)(3)); they are not independent of one another — the introductory clause's own condition (that the woman who gave birth is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage) applies to the refusal consequence quoted here. Section 7554(a) lists four other bases (identification under § 7555 that is not successfully challenged, an admission accepted by the court, default, and other evidence) on which a court may likewise find a person to be a parent; this clause addresses only the refusal basis and does not restate those other bases. Whether, and under what conditions, a refusal to submit to testing carries this consequence varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: The cost of genetic testing ordered under a court-appointed expert is not left unaddressed. Family Code § 7553(a) provides that the compensation of each court-appointed expert witness "shall be fixed at a reasonable amount" and paid as the court orders; except as provided in § 7553(b), the court may order it paid by the parties in proportions and at times the court sets, may order a party's proportion paid by the county, and may then tax all, part, or none of that amount as costs in the action. Section 7553(b) draws a distinct line for an expert appointed on the court's own motion rather than at a party's request: "If the expert witness is appointed for the court's needs, the compensation shall be paid by the court."

citations.cite: fixing and allocating a party-requested expert's compensation
citations.quote: The compensation of each expert witness appointed by the court shall be fixed at a reasonable amount. It shall be paid as the court shall order. Except as provided in subdivision (b), the court may order that it be paid by the parties in the proportions and at the times the court prescribes, or that the proportion of any party be paid by the county, and that, after payment by the parties or the county or both, all or part or none of it be taxed as costs in the action or proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7553(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court pays for an expert appointed for its own needs
citations.quote: If the expert witness is appointed for the court’s needs, the compensation shall be paid by the court.

Whether, and how, the cost of court-ordered genetic testing is allocated varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: A person can qualify as a presumed parent under Family Code § 7611 through several routes — marriage or an attempted marriage around the time of the child's birth, later marrying and being named on the birth certificate or undertaking support, or receiving the child into the home and openly holding the child out as the person's own. Section 7612(a) makes that presumption rebuttable, and only "by clear and convincing evidence." Where more than one of these presumptions could apply to Riley Lee, or where a § 7611 presumption conflicts with a claim by a person identified as a genetic parent under § 7555, § 7612(b) does not automatically favor genetic evidence: instead, "the presumption that on the facts is founded on the weightier considerations of policy and logic controls," and if one of the competing presumed parents is also a presumed parent under the marital-presumption statute (§ 7540), that particular presumption can only be rebutted through the § 7541 process described in this document's companion clause.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7612(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence
citations.quote: Except as provided in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 7540) and Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 7570) of Part 2, a presumption under Section 7611 is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof and may be rebutted in an appropriate action only by clear and convincing evidence.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7612(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the weightier-considerations standard for competing presumptions or genetic evidence
citations.quote: If two or more presumptions arise under Section 7611 that conflict with each other, or if one or more presumptions under Section 7611 conflict with a claim by a person identified as a genetic parent pursuant to Section 7555, the presumption that on the facts is founded on the weightier considerations of policy and logic controls. If one of the presumed parents is also a presumed parent under Section 7540, the presumption arising under Section 7540 may only be rebutted pursuant to Section 7541.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can resolve competing parentage presumptions — including a conflict with genetic-testing evidence — through a case-specific policy-and-logic balancing test rather than a fixed rule automatically favoring either the presumption or the genetic result, not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any such conflict would be resolved for, any specific child. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7612(a) and § 7612(b)); no additional independent source beyond § 7612 itself was found for the weightier-considerations standard. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: on the statute's actual text, a genetic-parent identification under § 7555 does not itself create a separate rebuttable or conclusive presumption that automatically controls over a conflicting § 7611 presumption — it is instead one input the court weighs under the same weightier-considerations balancing test used for conflicts between two § 7611 presumptions. Whether, and how, competing parentage presumptions and genetic evidence are reconciled varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: California's Uniform Parentage Act does not apply one single statute of limitations to every kind of parentage action; the timing rule depends on what is being asked of the court. Family Code § 7630(a)(1) allows an action "[a]t any time for the purpose of declaring the existence of" a presumed or established parent-child relationship regarding Riley Lee — no fixed filing deadline applies to establishing that relationship under this provision. By contrast, § 7630(a)(2) allows an action to declare the nonexistence of a § 7611(a)-(c) presumed relationship "only if the action is brought within a reasonable time after obtaining knowledge of relevant facts" — a flexible, fact-dependent limit rather than a fixed number of days or years. A different, fixed rule applies specifically to challenging the separate marital presumption under § 7540: as described in this document's companion clause, § 7541(b) requires that specific challenge to be filed and served within a hard two-year deadline running from the child's date of birth.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no fixed deadline to declare the existence of the relationship
citations.quote: At any time for the purpose of declaring the existence of the parent and child relationship presumed under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, or established pursuant to Section 7613.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the reasonable-time standard to declare nonexistence
citations.quote: For the purpose of declaring the nonexistence of the parent and child relationship presumed under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611 only if the action is brought within a reasonable time after obtaining knowledge of relevant facts. After the presumption has been rebutted, parentage of the child by another person may be determined in the same action, if that person has been made a party.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can apply different timing rules — no deadline, a flexible reasonable-time standard, and a fixed deadline — to different categories of parentage action within a single statutory scheme, not a claim about which state's law governs the timing of any specific petitioner's, respondent's, or alleged parent's claim. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7630(a)(1) and § 7630(a)(2)); the cross-reference to § 7541(b)'s two-year deadline is addressed independently, and in full, in this document's companion clause on the marital presumption, and is not re-quoted here. No general, catch-all limitations period for a § 7630(c) action to determine parentage (outside the marital-presumption and nonexistence-challenge categories addressed above) was located in the sections reviewed for this document; this document does not represent that no such rule exists elsewhere in California law, only that this research did not locate one within the sections reviewed. Whether, and how, a state limits the time to bring or challenge a parentage action varies substantially and is exactly the kind of date-sensitive fact that does not transfer across jurisdictions.
